title: Photorespiration, Drought and the Assimilation–Growth Gap: Bounding the Forgone Wood in High-Elevation Cedrus libani and Juniperus excelsa Forests of the Eastern Mediterranean
content: Türkiye holds the world's largest natural stands of Lebanon cedar (Cedrus libani A. Rich.) and extensive Crimean juniper forest (Juniperus excelsa M. Bieb.), together 884,361 ha of closed, drought-exposed forest. Both assimilate at needle water potentials near −3.0 MPa, yet lose some of their potential assimilation to photorespiration and stomatal closure under water deficit. A literature-parameterized scenario model relaxes both constraints against a radiation-limited ceiling. Zonal photorespiratory and stomatal input fractions of potential gross primary production (GPP) are 8%–16% and 14%–28%; after coupling, the model removes 13%–23% and 12%–23%. Together, these reduce weighted-mean net primary productivity from 3.29 to 2.14 Mg C ha−1 yr−1, a 34.9% reduction in potential GPP (Monte Carlo interval 31.7%–37.3%, conditional on the elicitation). Of that loss, 37%–45% is obligate photorespiration beyond management reach, depending on how the jointly caused interaction is assigned; the obligate share falls along the aridity gradient. Whether the loss becomes forgone wood is a separate question: radial growth in these species is confined to a narrow climatic window that does not coincide with peak assimilation. Under complete source control, the estate forgoes 1.5 million m3 and 3.7 million Mg CO2 annually, worth US$ 0.21 billion; under complete sink control, none.
